unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 4! In this unit you will explore probability – the mathematics of chance and likelihood. Every single day you meet events that might happen, that will surely happen, or that could never happen at all. When Amina wonders whether it will rain before she reaches school, when Yusuf flips a bottle cap to decide who kicks off the football match, or when Halima guesses which colour goat will come home first, they are all thinking about probability without even naming it.

concepts.title: The Language of Chance
concepts.explanation:
Probability begins with words. Before we ever use numbers, we describe how likely an event is using five special words. Learn them carefully, because you will use them throughout the whole unit.

Certain – the event will definitely happen. There is a 100% chance. Example: after Monday comes Tuesday.

Likely – the event will probably happen, but it is not guaranteed. Example: it will rain during the rainy season.

Even chance – the event is just as likely to happen as not to happen. There is a 50% chance, like flipping a coin.

Unlikely – the event probably will not happen, but it still might. Example: rolling a 6 on your very first try.

Impossible – the event cannot happen at all. There is a 0% chance. Example: a fish climbing a tree.

Notice how these words form a ladder from ‘no chance at all’ up to ‘completely sure’. Impossible sits at the very bottom, certain sits at the very top, and even chance sits right in the middle. Unlikely is low down but not at the bottom, and likely is high up but not at the top. Keeping this ladder in your mind helps you choose the right word for any event.

Let us look at more everyday examples so the words become solid. It is certain that if you drop a stone it will fall to the ground, because gravity always pulls objects down. It is likely that Hassan will have homework this week, because he usually does. There is an even chance of getting heads when you flip a fair coin, because there are only two equally likely results. It is unlikely that you will find a four-leaf clover on your walk home, because most clovers have only three leaves. And it is impossible to roll an 8 on a normal six-sided die, because the largest number on it is 6.
concepts.example: A word of care: unlikely does not mean ‘never’. Unlikely events still happen sometimes – that is exactly why we say ‘unlikely’ and not ‘impossible’. Finding a coin on the ground is unlikely on any single day, yet it does happen now and then. Keeping this difference clear will save you from a very common mistake.

concepts.title: The Probability Scale
concepts.explanation:
We can draw the ladder of chance as a line, and this line is called the probability scale. Picture a straight line. At the far left end we write Impossible. At the far right end we write Certain. Exactly in the middle we write Even chance. Between impossible and the middle we write Unlikely, and between the middle and certain we write Likely.

Impossible — Unlikely — Even chance — Likely — Certain. That is the scale, running from left (no chance) to right (sure to happen). Every event in the world can be placed somewhere along this line. The closer an event sits to the right end, the more likely it is; the closer to the left end, the less likely.

Let us place some events. ‘The sun will set this evening’ goes at the far right, on Certain. ‘A dog will speak English to you’ goes at the far left, on Impossible. ‘Rolling an even number on a die’ goes right in the middle, on Even chance, because three of the six numbers (2, 4, 6) are even and three are odd. ‘It will rain sometime this month during the rainy season’ goes towards the right, on Likely. ‘Drawing the exact ace of spades from a full deck on the first try’ goes towards the left, on Unlikely.
concepts.example: The probability scale is useful because it lets us compare events at a glance. If one event sits further right than another, it is more likely. Later in this unit we will discover that probability can also be written as a fraction – for example, an even chance is one half, written as 1/2. On the scale, impossible matches the fraction 0, certain matches 1, and even chance matches 1/2. This connection between words, the scale, and fractions is one of the most beautiful ideas in the whole unit.

concepts.title: Listing Outcomes
concepts.explanation:
An outcome is one possible result of an experiment. When we roll a die, flip a coin, or pick a marble, each thing that could happen is an outcome. To think clearly about probability, we first list all the possible outcomes – carefully, so that none is missed and none is counted twice.

When you flip a coin, there are exactly two possible outcomes: heads or tails. When you roll a normal die, there are six possible outcomes: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. When you pick a single card from a deck by colour, there are two outcomes: red or black. Listing outcomes is the first step in working out how likely each one is.

Once we have listed the outcomes, we can find the probability of an event as a fraction. The rule is: probability = number of ways the event can happen ÷ total number of outcomes. For example, the probability of rolling a 4 on a die is 1 out of 6, because only one of the six outcomes is a 4. The probability of rolling an even number is 3 out of 6 (the 2, 4 and 6), which is the same as 1/2 – an even chance.

Listing outcomes carefully protects you from errors. Suppose a bag holds 3 red marbles, 2 blue marbles and 1 green marble. The total number of marbles is 3 + 2 + 1 = 6, so there are six equally likely outcomes when you pick one without looking. The probability of picking red is 3 out of 6, blue is 2 out of 6, and green is 1 out of 6. Because 3 is the largest of these, red is the most likely colour, and because 1 is the smallest, green is the least likely. Every one of these facts came simply from listing and counting the outcomes.
concepts.example: We can even list the outcomes for two things at once. Imagine spinning a spinner with sections red and blue, and also flipping a coin. The outcomes are: red-heads, red-tails, blue-heads, blue-tails. There are four outcomes in all. Being able to list combined outcomes neatly is a skill you will build on in later years, so it is worth practising the tidy, no-gaps, no-repeats habit now.

concepts.title: Comparing Likelihoods
concepts.explanation:
Often we need to decide which of two events is more likely. The secret is to compare their probabilities. Think of each probability as a fraction – how many favourable outcomes out of the total – and the larger fraction wins.

Which is more likely: getting heads on a coin flip, or rolling a 6 on a die? The coin gives heads with probability 1 out of 2. The die gives a 6 with probability 1 out of 6. Since 1 out of 2 is greater than 1 out of 6, getting heads is more likely. You can feel this is right: there are fewer results to choose from on a coin, so each one is more likely.

Here is a helpful idea: the more possible outcomes there are, the less likely any single one becomes. A coin has just 2 outcomes, so each has a 1 in 2 chance. A die has 6 outcomes, so each has a 1 in 6 chance. A spinner with 10 equal sections has 10 outcomes, so each single colour has only a 1 in 10 chance. As the number of outcomes grows, each individual outcome shrinks in likelihood.

Let us compare a trickier pair. In a class of 30 children, 18 are girls and 12 are boys. If Khadija picks one child at random to answer a question, is it more likely to be a girl or a boy? There are 18 ways to pick a girl and 12 ways to pick a boy, out of 30 children. Because 18 is greater than 12, choosing a girl is more likely – a probability of 18 out of 30 for a girl against 12 out of 30 for a boy. Comparing the counts of favourable outcomes gives the answer at once.
concepts.example: One more: drawing a red card from a deck, or drawing a king? A deck has 26 red cards out of 52, so drawing red is 26 out of 52, which is one half. A deck has only 4 kings out of 52, so drawing a king is 4 out of 52. Because 26 is far greater than 4, drawing a red card is much more likely. Always look at how many favourable outcomes there are compared with the total, and the more likely event will stand out clearly.

concepts.title: Collecting and Using Data
concepts.explanation:
So far we have worked out probability by thinking – this is called theoretical probability. But we can also discover likelihood by collecting data from the real world. Data is information we gather by watching and counting, and a neat way to collect it is with a tally chart.

In a tally chart, each time something happens you draw a small mark. To make counting easy, you group the marks in fives: draw four straight marks, then cross them with a fifth mark to make a bundle of five. This means you can count quickly in fives at the end, instead of one by one.

Imagine Idris stands outside Nuur Academy and records the colours of cars that pass. After a while his tally chart shows: red 7, blue 5, silver 11, black 8, white 10, other 3. Adding these gives a total of 7 + 5 + 11 + 8 + 10 + 3 = 44 cars. Now the data can answer probability questions. The most common colour is silver (11 cars), so the next car is most likely to be silver. The likelihood of the next car being silver is 11 out of 44, and the likelihood of it being red is 7 out of 44. The likelihood of it being white or black together is 10 + 8 = 18 out of 44.

From data we can make predictions. Because silver was the most common colour, we would predict that silver cars are the most likely to pass, and that ‘other’ colours (only 3 out of 44) are the least likely. Predictions from data are sensible guesses, not guarantees – the very next car could easily break the pattern – but they are far better than guessing blindly.
concepts.example: There is one more vital idea: sample size. The more data you collect, the more reliable your predictions become. If Sahra watched only 5 cars and 3 were red, she might wrongly think most cars are red. But after watching 100 cars, she might find only 15 were red. The larger sample gives a truer picture. This is why careful mathematicians always try to collect plenty of data before trusting a pattern – a small sample can easily fool you.

concepts.title: Probability Experiments
concepts.explanation:
A probability experiment is an activity where we test how likely different outcomes really are. By running experiments we can check whether our predictions match what actually happens. To design a good experiment, follow six clear steps:

List all the possible outcomes.

Make a prediction about the likelihood of each outcome.

Decide how many times to repeat the experiment.

Make a tally chart to record the results.

Carry out the experiment and record what happens each time.

Compare the results with your prediction.

Here is an example. Suppose Omar wants to test whether a coin is fair. The outcomes are heads or tails. He predicts each has an even chance, about 50% each. He decides to flip the coin 50 times and record results in a tally chart. When he finishes, his chart shows 27 heads and 23 tails. His prediction was 25 and 25, so the result is close but not exact.

This is one of the most important lessons in the unit: experimental results rarely match the prediction exactly, especially with a small number of trials. Even a perfectly fair coin will not always give exactly half heads and half tails. Getting 27 and 23 instead of 25 and 25 does not mean the coin is unfair – it is just the normal wobble of chance. If Omar flipped the coin many hundreds more times, the fraction of heads would usually drift closer and closer to one half.

Experiments also help us judge fairness. A game or spinner is fair when every outcome has an equal chance. A spinner split into 4 equal sections – red, blue, green, yellow – is fair, because each colour has a 1 in 4 chance. But if the red section is made to fill half the spinner while the other three colours share the rest, the spinner is unfair: red now has a 1 in 2 chance, while blue, green and yellow each have only about 1 in 6. Running many spins and tallying the results would reveal red winning far more often than the others.

Finally, probability helps us make informed decisions. If the forecast gives an 80% chance of rain, Maryam sensibly carries an umbrella. If a game offers only a 1 in 100 chance of winning a prize, Ibrahim might decide it is not worth playing. If one route to school is likely to be less crowded, Yusuf chooses that route. Good decisions grow from a clear understanding of likelihood.

You have now met six big ideas: the language of chance, the probability scale, listing outcomes, comparing likelihoods, collecting and using data, and running probability experiments. These ideas are not separate islands – they work together. When Amina wonders whether her football team will win, she uses the language of chance to say ‘likely’, she could place that on the probability scale, and if she kept a record of past matches she would be collecting data to make a better prediction.
concepts.example: The best way to lock these ideas into your memory is to use them with real things around your home. Flip a bottle cap and tally heads and tails. List the outcomes when you pick fruit from a bowl with your eyes closed. Guess whether the next person to arrive for family dinner will be older or younger than you, then check. Every time you name a likelihood, list outcomes, or run a little experiment, your understanding of probability grows stronger, and the harder statistics you meet in later years will feel much easier. Now let us practise together with some worked examples.

methods.title: How to find a probability
methods.example: A bag holds 3 red, 2 blue and 1 green marble. What is the probability of picking blue?
steps: List all the possible outcomes.
Count how many outcomes are favourable (the ones you want).
Count the total number of outcomes.
Write the probability as favourable out of total, for example 2 out of 6.

methods.title: How to compare two likelihoods
methods.example: Put these in order from least likely to most likely: rolling a 6 on a die; the sun setting tonight; a fish climbing a tree.
steps: Work out each probability as a fraction (favourable out of total).
Compare the fractions – the larger one is more likely.
Remember: more possible outcomes means each single outcome is less likely.

methods.title: How to run a probability experiment
methods.example: A spinner is spun 40 times with results: red 14, blue 8, green 9, yellow 9. If it were fair, how many of each would you expect? Do you think it is fair? Explain.
steps: Decide what to test and list the outcomes.
Write a prediction before you start.
Repeat many times and tally the results.
Compare the results with your prediction, and remember small samples wobble.

methods.title: Compare two likelihoods
methods.example: Which is more likely: drawing a red card from a deck, or drawing a king?
steps: Red cards = 26 out of 52 = 1/2.
Kings = 4 out of 52.
Since 26 is much greater than 4, drawing a red card is more likely.

methods.title: Use a tally chart
methods.example: A spinner with red, blue, green and yellow is spun 40 times: red 14, blue 8, green 9, yellow 9. If the spinner were fair, how many times would each colour be expected, and does the data suggest it is fair?
steps: A fair spinner would give each colour 40 ÷ 4 = 10 spins.
Red appeared 14 times, well above 10, while the others were near it.
This suggests the spinner may not be completely fair — red seems to come up more often than expected.

methods.title: Judge fairness of a game
methods.example: Player 1 wins if a die shows 1, 2 or 3; Player 2 wins if it shows 4, 5 or 6. Is this game fair?
steps: Player 1 wins with 3 outcomes; Player 2 wins with 3 outcomes.
Both have a 3 out of 6 chance, which is 1/2 each.
The game is fair.

workedExamples.title: Choose the right chance word
workedExamples.prompt: Describe the likelihood of each event using certain, likely, even chance, unlikely or impossible: (a) the sun will rise tomorrow; (b) rolling a 7 on a normal die; (c) getting tails on a fair coin.
workedExamples.solution: (a) Certain – it happens every day. (b) Impossible – a die only has 1 to 6. (c) Even chance – there are two equally likely results, heads or tails, so tails has a 1 in 2 chance.

workedExamples.title: Place events on the scale
workedExamples.prompt: Put these in order from least likely to most likely: rolling a 6 on a die; the sun setting tonight; a fish climbing a tree.
workedExamples.solution: ‘A fish climbing a tree’ is impossible (least likely). ‘Rolling a 6’ is unlikely (1 in 6). ‘The sun setting tonight’ is certain (most likely). Order: fish climbing a tree, rolling a 6, the sun setting.

workedExamples.title: List outcomes and find a probability
workedExamples.prompt: A bag holds 3 red, 2 blue and 1 green marble. What is the probability of picking blue?
workedExamples.solution: Total marbles = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. Blue marbles = 2. So the probability of blue is 2 out of 6, which is the same as 1/3. Red (3 out of 6) is the most likely; green (1 out of 6) is the least likely.

workedExamples.title: Compare two likelihoods
workedExamples.prompt: Which is more likely: drawing a red card from a deck, or drawing a king?
workedExamples.solution: Red cards = 26 out of 52 = 1/2. Kings = 4 out of 52. Since 26 is much greater than 4, drawing a red card is more likely.

workedExamples.title: Use a tally chart
workedExamples.prompt: A spinner with red, blue, green and yellow is spun 40 times: red 14, blue 8, green 9, yellow 9. If the spinner were fair, how many times would each colour be expected, and does the data suggest it is fair?
workedExamples.solution: A fair spinner would give each colour 40 ÷ 4 = 10 spins. Red appeared 14 times, well above 10, while the others were near it. This suggests the spinner may not be completely fair — red seems to come up more often than expected.

workedExamples.title: Judge fairness of a game
workedExamples.prompt: Player 1 wins if a die shows 1, 2 or 3; Player 2 wins if it shows 4, 5 or 6. Is this game fair?
workedExamples.solution: Player 1 wins with 3 outcomes; Player 2 wins with 3 outcomes. Both have a 3 out of 6 chance, which is 1/2 each. The game is fair.

workedExamples.title: Make a prediction from data
workedExamples.prompt: Over 30 days in April, the weather was sunny 12 days, cloudy 10 days, rainy 8 days. What is the likelihood of a sunny day, and what might you predict for May 1st?
workedExamples.solution: Sunny days = 12 out of 30, which is 2/5 or 40%. Sunny was the most common, so you might predict a sunny day for May 1st. But this is only a sensible guess — weather changes, and one month of data is a small sample.

workedExamples.title: Spot the unfair spinner
workedExamples.prompt: A spinner is half red, one quarter blue and one quarter green. Player 1 wins on red; Player 2 wins on blue or green. Is it fair?
workedExamples.solution: Red covers 1/2 the spinner. Blue and green together cover 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. So Player 1 has a 1/2 chance and Player 2 has a 1/2 chance — the game is actually fair, even though it looks lopsided, because the two smaller sections add up to the big one.

workedExamples.title: Order these events from least likely to most likely…
workedExamples.prompt: Order these events from least likely to most likely: rolling a 6 on a die; finding a four-leaf clover; the sun setting tonight; rolling an even number.
workedExamples.solution: From least likely to most likely: finding a four-leaf clover, rolling a 6 on a die, rolling an even number on a die, the sun setting tonight.

workedExamples.title: A spinner has 5 equal sections numbered 1 to 5. What…
workedExamples.prompt: A spinner has 5 equal sections numbered 1 to 5. What is the probability of landing on 3? What is the probability of landing on an even number?
workedExamples.solution: Landing on 3 has a 1 out of 5 chance. Landing on an even number (2 or 4) has a 2 out of 5 chance.

workedExamples.title: In a class, 20 like football and 10 like swimming. Is…
workedExamples.prompt: In a class, 20 like football and 10 like swimming. Is a random child more likely to prefer football or swimming? Give the probability of each.
workedExamples.solution: Football is more likely — 20 out of 30 (2 out of 3) prefer football, compared with swimming at 10 out of 30 (1 out of 3).

workedExamples.solution: A fair spinner gives 40 ÷ 4 = 10 of each; red (14) is well above 10 while the rest are near it, so it may not be fair.

activities.title: Build a Probability Scale
activities.materials: a long strip of paper, a pencil, and a ruler.
steps: Draw a straight line across the paper. Write ‘Impossible’ at the left end and ‘Certain’ at the right end.
Mark ‘Even chance’ exactly in the middle, then ‘Unlikely’ and ‘Likely’ in between.
Think of eight everyday events and write each one on the scale where it belongs.
Show your scale to a family member and ask if they agree with where you placed each event.
Keep your scale – you can use it all through this unit to judge new events.

activities.title: The Great Coin-Flip Experiment
activities.materials: a coin (or a bottle cap) and a tally chart on paper.
steps: Predict how many heads and tails you will get in 50 flips. Write your prediction down.
Flip the coin 50 times, making a tally mark for heads or tails each time.
Count the totals and compare them with your prediction. How close were you?
Now flip another 50 times and add them on. Do the totals get closer to half and half?
This experiment shows why a larger number of trials gives a more reliable picture of a fair coin.

activities.title: Fair or Unfair? The Spinner Test
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and a paperclip to spin around a pencil point as a pointer.
steps: Draw a circle split into 4 equal sections coloured red, blue, green and yellow.
Predict how many times each colour will come up in 40 spins.
Spin 40 times and tally the results, then compare with your prediction.
Now draw a second spinner where red fills half the circle. Spin it 40 times and see how the results change.
Talk about which spinner is fair and which is unfair, using probability words.

activities.title: Marble Bag Investigation
activities.materials: a bag or cup and coloured stones or beans – for example 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green.
steps: List all the colours and how many of each, then work out the total.
Predict which colour you are most likely to pull out, and which least likely.
Without looking, pick one stone, record its colour, and put it back. Do this 30 times.
Compare your tally with your prediction. Did red come up most often, as expected?

activities.title: Design a Fair Game (Family Challenge)
activities.materials: a die or a spinner, and one or more family members to play with.
steps: Invent a two-player game where both players have an equal chance of winning.
Explain to your family why the game is fair, using probability language.
Now change one rule to make the game unfair. Who has the better chance now?
Play both versions and see whether the results feel fair or unfair.

activities.title: Real-World Data Hunt
activities.materials: a notebook and something to observe – cars, birds, or the colour of clothes people wear.
steps: Choose something to observe and decide how you will record it in a tally chart.
Watch and tally for a set time, grouping your marks in fives.
Add up the totals and work out which outcome was most and least common.
Use your data to predict what you would see next, then explain why a bigger sample is more reliable.

rules.title: The Five Chance Words
rules.text: Certain = sure to happen (100%). Impossible = cannot happen (0%). Likely = probably will. Unlikely = probably will not. Even chance = 50-50.

rules.title: The Probability Scale

rules.title: The Probability Rule
rules.text: Probability = number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes. Example: rolling an even number = 3 out of 6 = one half.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Collecting and Using Data.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: So far we have worked out probability by thinking – this is called theoretical probability. But we can also discover likelihood by collecting data from the real world. Data is information we gather by watching and counting, and a neat way to collect it is with a tally chart. In a tally chart, each time something happens you draw a small mark. To make counting easy, you group the marks in fives: draw four straight marks, then cross them with a fifth mark to make a bundle of five. This lets you count a large tally quickly in groups of five instead of counting every single mark one at a time.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Probability Experiments.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A probability experiment is an activity where we test how likely different outcomes really are, so we can check whether our predictions match what actually happens. A good experiment follows clear steps: list the possible outcomes, make a prediction about the likelihood of each outcome, decide how many times to repeat the experiment, carry it out and tally the results carefully, then compare the results with your prediction – remembering that a small number of trials can vary a lot from the theoretical probability.
